# OneCoin / “Cryptoqueen” Network: Public-Record Reconstruction

## Executive Summary

The publicly documented evidence describes OneCoin as an international investment-fraud scheme that marketed a purported cryptocurrency through a global multi-level-marketing (“MLM”) network. According to the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ), OneCoin Ltd. began operating in 2014 and was based in Sofia, Bulgaria. Between 2014 and 2019, its co-founders, Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood, together with others, allegedly obtained more than $4 billion from victims worldwide through misrepresentations about the cryptocurrency, its value, and its underlying technology. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

The available sources identify Ignatova and Greenwood as OneCoin’s principal co-founders. Greenwood’s documented role was more specifically described: he was allegedly OneCoin’s top MLM distributor, received 5% of monthly OneCoin sales, and earned more than $300 million. He was sentenced to 20 years in prison and ordered to forfeit approximately $300,000. ([S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

The evidence establishes enforcement actions against Greenwood and other OneCoin-related figures, as well as a DOJ-led asset-forfeiture remission process. More than $40 million in forfeited assets was reported as available for victim compensation as of April 13, 2026. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

The sources do not establish what happened to Ignatova. They state that she remains at large and is an FBI Top Ten Fugitive. Those facts establish her unresolved law-enforcement status, not her location, current condition, or whether she is alive. Assertions beyond that evidence should be treated as unverified.

## Source Identification and Reliability

For purposes of this report, the two supplied source records are identified as follows:

| Source ID | Source | Type | Principal evidentiary value |
|---|---|---|---|
| **S1** | U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs, “Justice Department Announces Compensation Process for OneCoin Fraud Victims With Funds Recovered Through Asset Forfeiture,” April 13, 2026 | Government press release | Current enforcement, victim-compensation, forfeiture, agency statements, scheme overview |
| **S2** | ArentFox Schiff, “Co-Founder of Fraudulent Cryptocurrency Sentenced to 20 Years in Prison,” September 15, 2023 | Law-firm legal analysis | Greenwood’s sentence, alleged operational mechanics, investor count, and prosecution-related summary |

S1 is the more authoritative source for current enforcement and compensation information because it is an official DOJ release. S2 is a secondary legal publication. It is useful for additional details concerning Greenwood’s sentence and the alleged mechanics of OneCoin, but its descriptions of the scheme should be read as a summary of government allegations and prosecution facts rather than as an independent investigative finding.

## Reconstruction of the OneCoin Scheme

### Formation and operating period

The DOJ states that OneCoin began operations in 2014 and was based in Sofia, Bulgaria. It marketed and sold a purported cryptocurrency called OneCoin through a global MLM structure. The documented period relevant to the fraud was 2014 through 2019. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

The law-firm account similarly states that OneCoin began operations in Bulgaria in 2014 and began operating in the United States around 2015. The evidence therefore supports a transnational operating model with Bulgarian origins and a later U.S. presence. ([S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

### Marketing and recruitment structure

OneCoin was marketed through a global MLM network. Under the structure described in the sources, members were encouraged to recruit additional participants and could receive commissions when others purchased OneCoin packages. This recruitment-based model was central to distribution and revenue generation. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

The evidence supports describing the MLM network as an alleged mechanism for selling investment packages and expanding the pool of participants. It does not, on the supplied record, establish the identity of all distributors, the precise legal status of every participant, or that every person in the network knowingly participated in fraud. Such distinctions are important because the sources describe a large international membership and investor base, but do not provide a participant-by-participant culpability analysis.

### Representations about value

According to the government allegations summarized by S2, OneCoin represented that its value was determined by market supply and demand. The prosecution account stated that the value was instead set arbitrarily without regard to genuine market forces. ([S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

This alleged misrepresentation is significant because it concerns the basic economic premise of the investment. A cryptocurrency marketed as having market-based value would ordinarily be understood by purchasers as subject to independent market forces. The evidence presented here indicates that prosecutors alleged OneCoin’s valuation was controlled rather than market-derived. The available sources do not provide a full valuation history or technical financial records, so the report does not independently quantify the difference between stated and actual value.

### Representations about blockchain technology

S2 reports that Greenwood claimed OneCoin had a private blockchain capable of identifying OneCoins and recording historical transactions. Prosecutors allegedly maintained that no publicly verifiable blockchain existed. ([S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

The distinction between a claimed private blockchain and the absence of a publicly verifiable blockchain is central to the technology-related allegations. The supplied sources do not provide technical specifications, source code, a chain ledger, or an independent forensic report. Accordingly, the supported conclusion is that prosecutors alleged the blockchain representations were false or materially misleading; the supplied material does not permit a more detailed technical reconstruction.

### Scale of the alleged fraud

The DOJ states that victims invested more than $4 billion worldwide. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)) S2 reports that the government charged Greenwood and others with obtaining more than $4 billion from approximately 3.5 million investors. ([S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

The $4 billion figure should be understood as the documented estimate of investments or victim losses attributed to the scheme, not as the amount currently recoverable. The DOJ reported that more than $40 million in forfeited assets was available for compensation in 2026. The difference between the alleged worldwide investment total and the available forfeited assets demonstrates that the compensation process could cover only a fraction of the alleged losses, subject to eligibility determinations and the final distribution calculation. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

## Principal Founders and Roles

### Ruja Ignatova

The DOJ identifies Ruja Ignatova as a co-founder of OneCoin Ltd. and states that she and Greenwood, along with others, orchestrated the international investment scheme. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

S2 identifies Ignatova as OneCoin’s other co-founder and states that she remains at large. It also reports that she was added to the FBI’s Top Ten Most Wanted List in June 2022. ([S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

The available evidence supports the following limited characterization:

- Ignatova was a principal co-founder of OneCoin.
- The DOJ attributes the scheme’s orchestration to Ignatova, Greenwood, and others.
- She is identified in the sources as a fugitive who remains at large.
- The sources do not establish her present location, physical condition, or whether she is alive.

The word “Cryptoqueen” is not needed to establish her role. It is a public nickname associated with her, but the supplied DOJ source refers to her by name and as a co-founder rather than relying on that label.

### Karl Sebastian Greenwood

Greenwood is identified as a co-founder of OneCoin and as a citizen of Sweden and the United Kingdom. ([S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

His operational role is described more specifically than Ignatova’s in the supplied evidence. He was allegedly the top MLM distributor for OneCoin and allegedly received 5% of monthly OneCoin sales. S2 states that this amounted to more than $300 million in earnings. ([S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

Greenwood’s enforcement status is established in the supplied evidence:

- He was sentenced to 20 years in prison.
- He was ordered to pay approximately $300,000 in forfeiture.
- The sentence concerned his role in the OneCoin fraud scheme.

S2 uses the phrase “alleged role” in describing the scheme, but it also states that Greenwood was sentenced. This report therefore treats the sentence as an enforcement fact while preserving the source’s allegation-based description of the underlying conduct.

## Enforcement and Asset Recovery

The DOJ states that it filed multiple OneCoin-related prosecutions in the Southern District of New York. Several key figures were sentenced, and the Department pursued criminal forfeiture of property derived from the alleged fraud proceeds. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

As of April 13, 2026, more than $40 million in forfeited assets was reported to be available for victim compensation. The DOJ opened a remission process for individuals who purchased OneCoin between 2014 and 2019 and stated that eligible individuals could submit petitions through the designated remission administrator, Kroll Settlement Administration LLC. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

The DOJ also stated that the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section manages the compensation process. It warned that neither the remission administrator nor the DOJ would ask victims to pay to participate. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered))

These facts establish an official recovery mechanism, but not the eventual percentage recovery for each victim. The sources do not state how many petitions will be filed, how eligibility will be calculated, or when final payments will be completed.

## Ignatova’s Status: Established Facts and Unresolved Claims

### Established by the supplied sources

The sources establish that:

1. Ignatova was a OneCoin co-founder.
2. The DOJ attributes the alleged scheme to her, Greenwood, and others.
3. She remains at large according to the supplied reports.
4. She was placed on the FBI’s Top Ten Most Wanted List in June 2022.
5. The FBI continues to seek information concerning her.

([S1](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered); [S2](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison))

### Not established by the supplied sources

The supplied evidence does not establish:

- Ignatova’s current location;
- whether she is alive or dead;
- whether she is being protected by a particular person or organization;
- whether reports of her death are true;
- whether she continues to direct any OneCoin-related activity;
- whether she has been arrested, despite the reports stating that she remains at large.

The correct evidentiary conclusion is therefore that Ignatova’s status remains unresolved beyond her official fugitive designation and the statement that she remains at large. Any more definite account would exceed the supplied evidence.

## Assessment

On the supplied record, OneCoin is best characterized as a large-scale alleged investment fraud presented as a cryptocurrency opportunity and distributed through an international MLM system. The principal founders were Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood. Greenwood’s role is more concretely documented as a top MLM distributor and major beneficiary of sales commissions, while Ignatova’s documented role is that of co-founder and alleged orchestrator. The enforcement record is clearest for Greenwood, who received a 20-year sentence and forfeiture order. The DOJ’s 2026 remission announcement confirms that criminal-forfeiture proceeds are being directed toward victims, but the available recovery is far below the alleged $4 billion invested.

The evidence does not support resolving the many public theories concerning Ignatova’s fate. The responsible conclusion is narrower: she is identified as a co-founder, remains wanted and at large according to the supplied sources, and her present location and condition are unknown on this record.

## Findings

### Finding 1: What was OneCoin?

OneCoin was marketed as a cryptocurrency but was allegedly sold through a global MLM investment structure involving misrepresentations about its value and blockchain technology.  
**Supporting entities:** OneCoin Ltd.; OneCoin investors; MLM network.  
**Source references:** S1, S2.

### Finding 2: When and where did the scheme operate?

The scheme began in Bulgaria in 2014, had a U.S. operating presence around 2015, and the relevant fraud period identified by the DOJ was 2014–2019.  
**Supporting entities:** OneCoin Ltd.; Bulgaria; United States.  
**Source references:** S1, S2.

### Finding 3: Who were the principal founders?

Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood were identified as OneCoin’s co-founders.  
**Supporting entities:** Ruja Ignatova; Karl Sebastian Greenwood; OneCoin Ltd.  
**Source references:** S1, S2.

### Finding 4: What was Greenwood’s documented role?

Greenwood was identified as OneCoin’s top MLM distributor and allegedly received 5% of monthly sales, totaling more than $300 million.  
**Supporting entities:** Karl Sebastian Greenwood; OneCoin MLM network.  
**Source references:** S2.

### Finding 5: What enforcement action was taken against Greenwood?

Greenwood was sentenced to 20 years in prison and ordered to forfeit approximately $300,000.  
**Supporting entities:** Karl Sebastian Greenwood; U.S. prosecution.  
**Source references:** S2.

### Finding 6: What is established about Ignatova’s status?

Ignatova remains at large and is identified as an FBI Top Ten Fugitive. Her location and physical condition are unresolved in the supplied sources.  
**Supporting entities:** Ruja Ignatova; FBI.  
**Source references:** S1, S2.

### Finding 7: What recovery process exists?

The DOJ announced a remission process for eligible OneCoin purchasers, supported by more than $40 million in forfeited assets available for victim compensation as of April 13, 2026.  
**Supporting entities:** DOJ; Criminal Division; Kroll Settlement Administration LLC; OneCoin victims.  
**Source references:** S1.

## References

ArentFox Schiff. (2023, September 15). *Co-founder of fraudulent cryptocurrency sentenced to 20 years in prison*. Investigations Blog. [https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison](https://www.afslaw.com/perspectives/investigations-blog/co-founder-fraudulent-cryptocurrency-sentenced-20-years-prison)

U.S. Department of Justice, Office of Public Affairs. (2026, April 13). *Justice Department announces compensation process for OneCoin fraud victims with funds recovered through asset forfeiture*. [https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-compensation-process-onecoin-fraud-victims-funds-recovered)

Benefits DOJ Vacancies Legal Careers at DOJ Our Offices Find Help Contact Us Search Breadcrumb Justice.gov Office of Public Affairs News Press Releases Justice Department Announces Compensation Process For OneCoin Fraud Victims With Funds Recovered Through Asset Forfeiture MENU News All News Blogs Photo Galleries Podcasts Press Releases Speeches Videos Archived Press Releases Archived News Press Release Justice Department Announces Compensation Process for OneCoin Fraud Victims With Funds Recovered Through Asset Forfeiture Monday, April 13, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs Today, the Department of Justice announced the beginning of the remission compensation process to provide recovery for victims of the international investment scheme involving OneCoin Ltd. Between 2014 and 2019, Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood, co-founders of OneCoin Ltd. (OneCoin), and others orchestrated a large, international cryptocurrency investment scheme defrauding investors from around the globe. OneCoin, which began operations in 2014 and was based in Sofia, Bulgaria, marketed and sold a fraudulent cryptocurrency by the same name through a global multi-level-marketing (MLM) network. As a result of misrepresentations made about OneCoin, victims invested over $4 billion worldwide in the fraudulent cryptocurrency. The Department of Justice filed a number of OneCoin-related prosecutions in the Southern District of New York. Several key figures involved in the scheme have been sentenced, and the Department pursued criminal forfeiture of property derived from the proceeds of the fraud scheme. More than $40 million in forfeited assets are currently available for victim compensation. Through the remission process, victims who purchased the fraudulent OneCoin cryptocurrency between 2014 and 2019 may be eligible for compensation. Individuals who believe they may be victims may obtain a petition form online at www.onecoinremission.com . Victims may also call, email, or write to the Remission Administrator to request that a Petition Form be sent to them. The deadline for filing a petition is June 30. The Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section manages the remission compensation process. “Victims are at the core of everything we do at the Department of Justice,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department's Criminal Division. “As we did in this complex investment fraud case, the Department pursues forfeiture to take the profit out of crime and then use that money to compensate victims wherever possible. I commend the efforts of our colleagues in the Southern District of New York, our law enforcement partners, and our Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section, which manages the Asset Forfeiture Program, for all of their work on behalf of the victims in this important case.” “Between 2014 and 2019, OneCoin’s founders sold a lie disguised as cryptocurrency, costing victims more than $4 billion worldwide,” said U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton for the Southern District of New York. “Today’s announcement marks an important step toward returning funds to those harmed. While no recovery can fully undo the damage, our Office will continue working to seize criminal proceeds and prioritize getting money back into the hands of victims. If you believe you may be a victim of OneCoin, you may obtain a petition form online at www.onecoinremission.com.” “The victim losses accrued in this case are monumental,” said Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle Jr of the FBI New York Field Office. “Misled by falsified statements and empty promises, many unknowingly depleted their savings for a fraudulent investment scheme in an emerging financial ecosystem that would never pay out. With the unwavering support from the Department of Justice, the FBI maintains its commitment to returning these stolen funds to their rightful owners. Our office will continue its investigative pursuit of these criminal fraudsters — especially locating Ruja Ignatova, an FBI Top Ten Fugitive — alongside our partners at the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI) and the Southern District of New York. Any information concerning this fugitive can be submitted online at tips.fbi.gov or via our tipline at 1-800-CALL-FBI.” “The victims of the OneCoin scheme were misled and financially devastated by promises that were never real,” said Special Agent in Charge Jenifer L. Piovesan of IRS-CI. “Alongside our law enforcement partners, we worked tirelessly to trace illicit funds and recover them for victims. This compensation process represents a critical step toward returning stolen assets to those who were deceived. IRS-CI remains steadfast in its mission to follow the money and dismantle complex financial fraud schemes like OneCoin.” More information regarding the remission process, including eligibility criteria, updates, and frequently asked questions are available at www.onecoinremission.com or by calling 1-833-421-9748. Kroll Settlement Administration LLC is serving as the remission administrator in this matter. The FBI and IRS-CI conducted the criminal fraud investigation. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs (OIA) provided significant assistance. The Department of Justice, through the Asset Forfeiture Program, works diligently to compensate victims of crime. Since 2000, the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section (MNF), which oversees the Asset Forfeiture Program’s victim compensation program, has returned more than $12.5 billion in forfeited assets to victims of crime. MNF Attorney Advisor Drew Halter with the section’s Program Management and Training Unit is leading the remission process. Neither the Remission Administrator nor the Department of Justice will ask for any payment to participate in this remission process. Please be cautious of any individual or organization claiming to represent the Remission Administrator or the federal government in this matter. If you are a victim, any communications will come directly from the Remission Administrator or from government representatives with whom you have already had contact. Brater , Nadia Patel , Michael F. Dearington Share This Page Email LinkedIn X Facebook Headlines that Matter for Companies and Executives in Regulated Industries Off Co-Founder of Fraudulent Cryptocurrency Sentenced to 20 Years in Prison Karl Sebastian Greenwood, a citizen of Sweden and the United Kingdom and co-founder of the cryptocurrency OneCoin, was sentenced to 20 years in prison for his alleged role in a $4 billion fraud scheme. As described by prosecutors, OneCoin began operations in Bulgaria in 2014 and sold a fraudulent cryptocurrency with the same name through a multi-level-marketing (MLM) scheme. Around 2015, OneCoin began operating in the United States. The government charged Greenwood and others with making various misrepresentations about OneCoin to secure over $4 billion in investments from approximately 3.5 million investors. These alleged misrepresentations include claiming that OneCoin’s value was based on market supply and demand though the value was actually set arbitrarily without regard to market forces. Greenwood also claimed to have a private blockchain to identify OneCoins and record historical transactions, when no public verifiable blockchain actually existed. According to the government, OneCoin marketed its cryptocurrency through a global MLM network whereby OneCoin members would receive commissions for recruiting others to purchase cryptocurrency packages. As OneCoin’s top MLM distributor, Greenwood is alleged to have earned 5% of monthly OneCoin sales, totaling over $300 million. In addition to his 20-year prison term, Greenwood was ordered to pay approximately $300,000 in forfeiture. OneCoin’s other co-founder, Ruja Ignatova, remains at large and was added to the FBI’s Top Ten Most Wanted List in June 2022. A link to the US Department of Justice’s (DOJ) press release can be found here. Prison Inmate Pleads Guilty in COVID-19 Relief Fraud Telvin Breaux, an inmate in a California prison, and three other co-defendants pleaded guilty to conspiracy and aggravated identity theft charges for their alleged roles in a $25 million unemployment benefits scheme. According to the DOJ, Breaux and his co-defendants obtained personal identifying information of other inmates, as well as patients and customers at hospitals, dentists’ offices, and other businesses where one of the co-defendants worked or had connections. Breaux and his co-defendants then used this information to submit fraudulent unemployment insurance claims to the California Employment Development Department (EDD). In connection with these false claims, Breaux and his co-defendants also made specific misrepresentations that the individuals whose information they stole were unable to work as a result of the COVID-19 pandemic. In total, defendants are alleged to have submitted over 400 fraudulent claims totaling over $25 million to the EDD, $5.4 million of which was actually paid out and used by the defendants to purchase luxury vehicles, fund trips to Las Vegas, and pay rent and tuition. Each defendant faces a maximum of 22 years imprisonment as well as fines of $250,000. A link to the DOJ’s press release can be found here. Former NYC Non-Profit Finance Director Sentenced to 18 Months Imprisonment Donna Murray, the former finance director of a New York City-based nonprofit financial services trade association with over 600 members, was sentenced to 18 months imprisonment for allegedly embezzling nearly half a million dollars from the nonprofit. The government alleges that Murray was the nonprofit’s sole finance department employee and was responsible for maintaining the organization’s books and records, handling accounts receivable and payable, and managing financial statements to outside auditors. In addition, Murray is alleged to have been the only employee with the ability to make wire transfers for the organization. As detailed in the DOJ’s information, Murray was charged with a months-long embezzlement scheme in which she stole over $488,000 from the organization’s bank accounts through 105 unauthorized wire transfers to her personal account. Murray covered up the scheme by creating false entries in the organizations general ledger and transferring less than $10,000 in each transaction to avoid triggering bank reporting requirements. Prosecutors charged Murray with using the misappropriated funds to pay personal loans and purchase luxury items. For her conduct, Murray was sentenced to 18 months in prison. A link to the DOJ’s press release can be found here. Contacts D. Jacques Smith Partner and Investigations Practice Leader Randall A. Benefits DOJ Vacancies Legal Careers at DOJ Our Offices Find Help Contact Us Search Breadcrumb Justice.gov Office of Public Affairs News Press Releases Justice Department Announces Compensation Process For OneCoin Fraud Victims With Funds Recovered Through Asset Forfeiture MENU News All News Blogs Photo Galleries Podcasts Press Releases Speeches Videos Archived Press Releases Archived News Press Release Justice Department Announces Compensation Process for OneCoin Fraud Victims With Funds Recovered Through Asset Forfeiture Monday, April 13, 2026 Share Facebook X LinkedIn Email For Immediate Release Office of Public Affairs Today, the Department of Justice announced the beginning of the remission compensation process to provide recovery for victims of the international investment scheme involving OneCoin Ltd. Between 2014 and 2019, Ruja Ignatova and Karl Sebastian Greenwood, co-founders of OneCoin Ltd. (OneCoin), and others orchestrated a large, international cryptocurrency investment scheme defrauding investors from around the globe. OneCoin, which began operations in 2014 and was based in Sofia, Bulgaria, marketed and sold a fraudulent cryptocurrency by the same name through a global multi-level-marketing (MLM) network. As a result of misrepresentations made about OneCoin, victims invested over $4 billion worldwide in the fraudulent cryptocurrency. The Department of Justice filed a number of OneCoin-related prosecutions in the Southern District of New York. Several key figures involved in the scheme have been sentenced, and the Department pursued criminal forfeiture of property derived from the proceeds of the fraud scheme. More than $40 million in forfeited assets are currently available for victim compensation. Through the remission process, victims who purchased the fraudulent OneCoin cryptocurrency between 2014 and 2019 may be eligible for compensation. Individuals who believe they may be victims may obtain a petition form online at www.onecoinremission.com . Victims may also call, email, or write to the Remission Administrator to request that a Petition Form be sent to them. The deadline for filing a petition is June 30. The Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section manages the remission compensation process. “Victims are at the core of everything we do at the Department of Justice,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department's Criminal Division. “As we did in this complex investment fraud case, the Department pursues forfeiture to take the profit out of crime and then use that money to compensate victims wherever possible. I commend the efforts of our colleagues in the Southern District of New York, our law enforcement partners, and our Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section, which manages the Asset Forfeiture Program, for all of their work on behalf of the victims in this important case.” “Between 2014 and 2019, OneCoin’s founders sold a lie disguised as cryptocurrency, costing victims more than $4 billion worldwide,” said U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton for the Southern District of New York. “Today’s announcement marks an important step toward returning funds to those harmed. While no recovery can fully undo the damage, our Office will continue working to seize criminal proceeds and prioritize getting money back into the hands of victims. If you believe you may be a victim of OneCoin, you may obtain a petition form online at www.onecoinremission.com.” “The victim losses accrued in this case are monumental,” said Assistant Director in Charge James C. Barnacle Jr of the FBI New York Field Office. “Misled by falsified statements and empty promises, many unknowingly depleted their savings for a fraudulent investment scheme in an emerging financial ecosystem that would never pay out. With the unwavering support from the Department of Justice, the FBI maintains its commitment to returning these stolen funds to their rightful owners. Our office will continue its investigative pursuit of these criminal fraudsters — especially locating Ruja Ignatova, an FBI Top Ten Fugitive — alongside our partners at the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation (IRS-CI) and the Southern District of New York. Any information concerning this fugitive can be submitted online at tips.fbi.gov or via our tipline at 1-800-CALL-FBI.” “The victims of the OneCoin scheme were misled and financially devastated by promises that were never real,” said Special Agent in Charge Jenifer L. Piovesan of IRS-CI. “Alongside our law enforcement partners, we worked tirelessly to trace illicit funds and recover them for victims. This compensation process represents a critical step toward returning stolen assets to those who were deceived. IRS-CI remains steadfast in its mission to follow the money and dismantle complex financial fraud schemes like OneCoin.” More information regarding the remission process, including eligibility criteria, updates, and frequently asked questions are available at www.onecoinremission.com or by calling 1-833-421-9748. Kroll Settlement Administration LLC is serving as the remission administrator in this matter. The FBI and IRS-CI conducted the criminal fraud investigation. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs (OIA) provided significant assistance. The Department of Justice, through the Asset Forfeiture Program, works diligently to compensate victims of crime. Since 2000, the Criminal Division’s Money Laundering, Narcotics and Forfeiture Section (MNF), which oversees the Asset Forfeiture Program’s victim compensation program, has returned more than $12.5 billion in forfeited assets to victims of crime. MNF Attorney Advisor Drew Halter with the section’s Program Management and Training Unit is leading the remission process. Neither the Remission Administrator nor the Department of Justice will ask for any payment to participate in this remission process. Please be cautious of any individual or organization claiming to represent the Remission Administrator or the federal government in this matter. If you are a victim, any communications will come directly from the Remission Administrator or from government representatives with whom you have already had contact.
